paragraphs: Westmorland and Furness Council runs its fostering service jointly with Cumberland Council as Cumbria Fostering, so children in care here are looked after by that shared service and by independent agencies, including those shown above. In January 2026 the council said more than 700 children in Cumbria were in care.

That month Cumbria Fostering launched a campaign to tackle the myths that put people off. The council says there is no upper age limit as long as you are fit and healthy enough, that you can foster while working full or part time, that LGBTQ+ people are welcome, and that a disability or long-term health condition does not rule you out on its own; each application is looked at individually. You need a spare room and a way of life with space for a child.

The council lists what its carers receive: fees based on experience, availability and the number of children you look after, an allowance for each child's everyday costs, retainer payments for up to eight weeks a year without a child, help with set-up costs such as beds and uniforms, and mileage for approved journeys. Support includes your own social worker, a 24-hour support line, peer mentoring and support groups, therapeutic support, membership of The Fostering Network and a Mockingbird group. Training starts with the Skills to Foster course and continues online and in person at venues around Cumbria.

First enquiries can go through Foster With Us, a recruitment hub the council launched in July 2024 with Cumberland, Lancashire, Blackpool and Blackburn with Darwen councils. Cumbria Fostering holds information events through the year; its January 2026 campaign included sessions at Kendal Library and Barrow Library and one online.
Talk to the council and to two or three of the agencies above, and ask each how much travel is involved in your part of the area and what local support you would have.
